lessons.title: Choosing the right table, graph or chart
lessons.html:
Matching the form to the message

Farms and extension offices collect a great deal of data: rainfall, milk yields, weaning weights, crop yields, input costs, attendance at farmer days, tick counts. Raw numbers in a notebook help nobody until they are organised and shown in a form that answers a question. The first step is to decide what question you want the data to answer, then choose the form that shows it best.

PurposeBest formFarm example
Show exact values for referenceTableMonthly rainfall per camp
Compare categoriesBar or column chartMaize yield of five cultivars on a demo plot
Show change over timeLine graphDaily milk yield over a lactation
Show parts of a wholePie chart (few categories) or stacked barShare of costs: feed, labour, vet, fuel
Show a relationship between two measuresScatter plotFertiliser rate against yield
Show a process or sequenceFlow diagramSteps from milking to bulk tank to collection
Show where things areMap or sketch planLocation of boreholes and water points

Things to consider

  • Audience: farmers at a meeting may prefer a simple bar chart drawn on a flip chart; a manager may want a table with exact figures.
  • Type of data: categories (breeds, cultivars) or continuous measures (mass, litres, rand).
  • Amount of data: a pie chart with twelve slices is unreadable; use a bar chart instead.
  • Medium: printed report, slide, poster, phone screen.

A wrong choice can hide the message. A pie chart cannot show that milk yield is dropping month by month; a line graph shows it immediately.

lessons.title: Building accurate tables and graphs
lessons.html:
Developing the display

Before drawing anything, check the data. Look for missing values, obvious typing errors (a cow giving 250 litres a day) and inconsistent units (kilograms mixed with tonnes). Decide how to deal with gaps and note it.

Good tables

  • A clear title saying what, where and when: Weaning weights, Ntabeni communal herd, 2025 calf crop.
  • Column headings with units: Mass (kg), Price (R/kg).
  • Logical order of rows, for example by date or from highest to lowest.
  • Totals and averages where useful, clearly labelled.
  • The source of the data noted under the table.

Good graphs

  1. Title that states the message or content.
  2. Both axes labelled with units; the time axis is usually horizontal.
  3. Scales that start at zero for bar charts, so bars are not exaggerated.
  4. Even intervals on the scale.
  5. A legend if there is more than one data series.
  6. No unnecessary decoration: avoid 3D effects and heavy colours that distract.

Calculations you will often use

MeasureHowUse
Mean (average)Total divided by number of valuesAverage yield per hectare
MedianMiddle value when sortedTypical farm income when a few farms are very large
RangeHighest minus lowestSpread of weaning weights
PercentagePart divided by whole, times 100Calving percentage
Percentage change(New minus old) divided by old, times 100Change in feed cost year on year

Example: 46 calves weaned from 60 cows mated gives 46 divided by 60 times 100, which is about 77 percent weaning rate. Spreadsheet programs such as Excel or Google Sheets do these calculations and draw charts quickly, but you must still check that the formula and the chart are correct.

lessons.title: Analysing information and presenting conclusions
lessons.html:
From display to conclusion

Analysis means looking at the table or graph and asking what it tells you. Look for:

  • Trends: rising, falling or stable over time.
  • Comparisons: which group, cultivar or camp performs best or worst.
  • Patterns: seasonal peaks, such as tick numbers rising in summer.
  • Outliers: values far from the rest, which may be errors or important events such as a hailstorm.
  • Relationships: does yield rise with fertiliser rate, and does it level off?

Drawing sound conclusions

  1. State only what the data supports. If two demo plots differ by 0.2 t/ha in one season, that may be chance, not proof that one cultivar is better.
  2. Remember that a relationship is not always cause and effect. Farms with more tractors may have higher yields because they are also larger and better funded.
  3. Consider the context: rainfall, disease outbreaks, price changes.
  4. Mention the limits of the data: small sample, one season, missing months.
  5. Link the conclusion to a recommendation or decision.

Presenting the information

Present the message first, then the evidence. For example: Calving percentage in the group fell from 68 percent to 55 percent after the drought; the graph shows the drop matches the fall in body condition scores at mating. We recommend supplementary feeding of cows before the next breeding season.

  • Use one main message per slide or chart.
  • Talk the audience through the graph: what the axes show, then what to notice.
  • For farmer groups, use large, simple charts and real objects; translate key terms.
  • Place tables and graphs close to the text that discusses them and number them.
  • Be honest: never change scales or leave out data to make results look better.

Key points

  • Choose the form that answers the question: tables for exact values, bars for comparisons, lines for trends.
  • Check data for errors and consistent units before building displays.
  • Label titles, axes, units and sources clearly; start bar charts at zero.
  • Look for trends, comparisons, patterns, outliers and relationships.
  • State conclusions the data supports, note limits and link them to decisions.
